medical.title: New evidence questions benefits of turmeric for knee arthritis
medical.summary: A new Cochrane review has found that turmeric supplements may provide little or no clinically important pain relief for people with knee osteoarthritis, challenging conclusions from earlier research that suggested a benefit. The work appears in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

medical.title: Analysis of over 69,000 younger patients questions one-size-fits-all cutoff for colorectal cancer stool test
medical.summary: A new study led by experts at the University of Nottingham has provided new insight into how a commonly used test for colorectal cancer performs in people under 50.

medical.title: How research paved the way for progress in a rare form of ALS
medical.summary: An experimental ALS drug that grew out of basic and clinical research at Columbia University's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons may soon become available for patients with a rare and aggressive form of the disease.

medical.title: No clear benefit from two drugs intended to increase spontaneous birth after induction in first-time moms
medical.summary: There is no clear evidence that hyoscine butylbromide or sodium bicarbonate improves spontaneous vaginal birth rates (without the assistance of forceps or vacuum) in first-time moms after induction of labor, finds a large Norwegian trial published by The BMJ. Although small benefits of either drug can't be entirely ruled out, the researchers say the findings do not support their routine use.

medical.title: Morphea linked to higher risk for cancer
medical.summary: Morphea is associated with excess cancer incidence, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

medical.title: Creatine supplement use nearly doubles among US college students, new study finds
medical.summary: The use of creatine and protein supplements among U.S. college and university students has increased significantly over a five-year period, according to new research published in the journal Performance Enhancement & Health and led by researchers at the University of Toronto.

medical.title: How to relieve a stress headache (and keep the next one away)
medical.summary: You had a rough day at work and got stuck in traffic on the way home, and suddenly your head starts to ache.

medical.title: Brepocitinib yields improvements in cutaneous sarcoidosis
medical.summary: For patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis (CS), brepocitinib is associated with dose-dependent and clinically meaningful improvements, according to a study published online in JAMA Dermatology to coincide with the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

medical.title: FDA approves drug for infantile-onset Niemann-Pick type C after analysis finds longer survival
medical.summary: Researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and their collaborators at Beren Therapeutics, Thousand Oaks, California, have developed a treatment for infants with Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) disease, which is a rare and rapidly fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disorder. The drug, known as cyclodextrin (brand name Adrabetadex), extended the survival of participants with NPC in a large, international clinical trial and represents foundational scientific research efforts that began 20 years ago. The drug was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Nov. 17, 2026.

medical.title: Targeting immune overactivity in Down syndrome shows promise in phase 2 clinical trial
medical.summary: In a first-of-its-kind clinical trial, researchers at the Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome (Crnic Institute) at the University of Colorado Anschutz found that a medication targeting immune overactivity in people with Down syndrome reduced underlying inflammation and was associated with improvements in inflammatory skin conditions, while opening new avenues for research on brain health and Alzheimer's disease.

medical.title: Acupuncture‑like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
medical.summary: A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.

medical.title: Blood test may reveal which lymphoma patients will respond to immunotherapy
medical.summary: Cornell engineers and Dana-Farber oncologists found that RNA floating in the plasma carries a signature of a lymphoma tumor's surroundings, one that tracked with whether patients were still in remission a year later.

medical.title: Milkshake study offers clues to diet's brain effects in young adults
medical.summary: Results from a Virginia Tech eating trial add to evidence that the developing brain responds differently to foods that have been through industrial processing or contain ingredients not found in a home kitchen.

medical.title: Migraine and smoking associated with increased risk of stroke by age 60
medical.summary: Migraine and smoking were each associated with a higher risk of early stroke in people who had given birth, while participants with both had the highest risk, according to a study published in Neurology. The study defined early stroke as occurring at age 60 or younger.

medical.title: Brain changes in women during pregnancy may be key in finding MS cure
medical.summary: The very thing that worried doctors about women with multiple sclerosis (MS) in pregnancy could be what leads them to a cure. Researcher-clinicians at The Alfred and Monash University conducted a study to understand the nature of decreased brain volume occurring in pregnant women with MS, out of concern that the changes are a sign of disease progression.

science.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
science.summary: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

science.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
science.summary: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

science.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
science.summary: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.

science.title: Should we save every old building?
science.summary: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.

science.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
science.summary: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

science.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
science.summary: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

science.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
science.summary: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

science.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
science.summary: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.

science.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
science.summary: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

science.title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation
science.summary: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.

science.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
science.summary: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

science.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
science.summary: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

science.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
science.summary: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

science.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
science.summary: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

science.title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species
science.summary: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.

science.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
science.summary: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

science.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
science.summary: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

science.title: NASA Sets Coverage for Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Launch, Prelaunch
science.summary: NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23. Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus […]

science.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
science.summary: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

science.title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal
science.summary: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.

science.title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters
science.summary: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.

science.title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
science.summary: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

science.title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst
science.summary: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection.

science.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
science.summary: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

science.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
science.summary: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.

environment.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
environment.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

environment.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

environment.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
environment.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

environment.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
environment.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

environment.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

environment.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
environment.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

environment.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
environment.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

environment.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

environment.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

environment.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
environment.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.

mix_items.title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history
mix_items.summary: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks
mix_items.summary: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.

mix_items.title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites
mix_items.summary: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.

mix_items.title: New evidence questions benefits of turmeric for knee arthritis
mix_items.summary: A new Cochrane review has found that turmeric supplements may provide little or no clinically important pain relief for people with knee osteoarthritis, challenging conclusions from earlier research that suggested a benefit. The work appears in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.

mix_items.title: Should we save every old building?
mix_items.summary: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.

mix_items.title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold
mix_items.summary: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.

mix_items.title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline
mix_items.summary: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.

mix_items.title: Analysis of over 69,000 younger patients questions one-size-fits-all cutoff for colorectal cancer stool test
mix_items.summary: A new study led by experts at the University of Nottingham has provided new insight into how a commonly used test for colorectal cancer performs in people under 50.

mix_items.title: How research paved the way for progress in a rare form of ALS
mix_items.summary: An experimental ALS drug that grew out of basic and clinical research at Columbia University's Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons may soon become available for patients with a rare and aggressive form of the disease.

mix_items.title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb
mix_items.summary: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores
mix_items.summary: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.

mix_items.title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions
mix_items.summary: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.

mix_items.title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation
mix_items.summary: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.

mix_items.title: No clear benefit from two drugs intended to increase spontaneous birth after induction in first-time moms
mix_items.summary: There is no clear evidence that hyoscine butylbromide or sodium bicarbonate improves spontaneous vaginal birth rates (without the assistance of forceps or vacuum) in first-time moms after induction of labor, finds a large Norwegian trial published by The BMJ. Although small benefits of either drug can't be entirely ruled out, the researchers say the findings do not support their routine use.

mix_items.title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star
mix_items.summary: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.

mix_items.title: Morphea linked to higher risk for cancer
mix_items.summary: Morphea is associated with excess cancer incidence, according to a study published online Nov. 11 in JAMA Dermatology.

mix_items.title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats
mix_items.summary: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.

mix_items.title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views
mix_items.summary: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.

mix_items.title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins
mix_items.summary: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.

mix_items.title: Creatine supplement use nearly doubles among US college students, new study finds
mix_items.summary: The use of creatine and protein supplements among U.S. college and university students has increased significantly over a five-year period, according to new research published in the journal Performance Enhancement & Health and led by researchers at the University of Toronto.

mix_items.title: How to relieve a stress headache (and keep the next one away)
mix_items.summary: You had a rough day at work and got stuck in traffic on the way home, and suddenly your head starts to ache.

mix_items.title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species
mix_items.summary: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.

mix_items.title: Brepocitinib yields improvements in cutaneous sarcoidosis
mix_items.summary: For patients with cutaneous sarcoidosis (CS), brepocitinib is associated with dose-dependent and clinically meaningful improvements, according to a study published online in JAMA Dermatology to coincide with the annual meeting of the American College of Rheumatology, held from Nov. 6 to 11 in Orlando, Florida.

mix_items.title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome
mix_items.summary: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.

mix_items.title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold
mix_items.summary: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.

mix_items.summary: NASA, Northrop Grumman, and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than 10:47 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, for the next launch delivering science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. The agency also will hold a prelaunch media teleconference on Monday, Nov. 23. Filled with approximately 11,000 pounds of cargo, the Northrop Grumman Cygnus […]

mix_items.title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance
mix_items.summary: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?

mix_items.title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal
mix_items.summary: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.

mix_items.title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters
mix_items.summary: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.

mix_items.title: FDA approves drug for infantile-onset Niemann-Pick type C after analysis finds longer survival
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and their collaborators at Beren Therapeutics, Thousand Oaks, California, have developed a treatment for infants with Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) disease, which is a rare and rapidly fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disorder. The drug, known as cyclodextrin (brand name Adrabetadex), extended the survival of participants with NPC in a large, international clinical trial and represents foundational scientific research efforts that began 20 years ago. The drug was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on Nov. 17, 2026.

mix_items.title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?
mix_items.summary: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.

mix_items.title: Targeting immune overactivity in Down syndrome shows promise in phase 2 clinical trial
mix_items.summary: In a first-of-its-kind clinical trial, researchers at the Linda Crnic Institute for Down Syndrome (Crnic Institute) at the University of Colorado Anschutz found that a medication targeting immune overactivity in people with Down syndrome reduced underlying inflammation and was associated with improvements in inflammatory skin conditions, while opening new avenues for research on brain health and Alzheimer's disease.

mix_items.title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst
mix_items.summary: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection.

mix_items.title: Acupuncture‑like treatment linked to sustained weight loss in new study
mix_items.summary: A form of acupuncture that leaves dissolvable threads under the skin may help people lose weight, a small trial in China suggests.

mix_items.title: Blood test may reveal which lymphoma patients will respond to immunotherapy
mix_items.summary: Cornell engineers and Dana-Farber oncologists found that RNA floating in the plasma carries a signature of a lymphoma tumor's surroundings, one that tracked with whether patients were still in remission a year later.

mix_items.title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control
mix_items.summary: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.

mix_items.title: Milkshake study offers clues to diet's brain effects in young adults
mix_items.summary: Results from a Virginia Tech eating trial add to evidence that the developing brain responds differently to foods that have been through industrial processing or contain ingredients not found in a home kitchen.

mix_items.title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea
mix_items.summary: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.

mix_items.title: Migraine and smoking associated with increased risk of stroke by age 60
mix_items.summary: Migraine and smoking were each associated with a higher risk of early stroke in people who had given birth, while participants with both had the highest risk, according to a study published in Neurology. The study defined early stroke as occurring at age 60 or younger.

mix_items.title: Brain changes in women during pregnancy may be key in finding MS cure
mix_items.summary: The very thing that worried doctors about women with multiple sclerosis (MS) in pregnancy could be what leads them to a cure. Researcher-clinicians at The Alfred and Monash University conducted a study to understand the nature of decreased brain volume occurring in pregnant women with MS, out of concern that the changes are a sign of disease progression.

mix_items.title: Payment scheme for human-wildlife coexistence faces growing criticism from Sámi reindeer herders
mix_items.summary: A Swedish compensation scheme designed to encourage coexistence between reindeer herders and carnivores is facing growing criticism from Indigenous Sámi communities. Inadequate payments, deficient monitoring methods and lack of meaningful dialogue between authorities and reindeer herders are eroding trust in the system, researchers tell Mongabay. “The state of Sweden hasn’t actually understood how severe and […]

mix_items.summary: Readers are certainly familiar with the Mother Nature Cambodia 5 (MNC5) after Mongabay released its documentary The Clearing in July 2025, chronicling the hopes, activism, and commitment of the group. The film detailed their lives while free on bail awaiting a likely guilty verdict for “plotting against the government” by fighting to protect Cambodia’s natural […]

mix_items.title: Rising preterm births in Bangladesh linked to extreme heat, research suggests
mix_items.summary: Hafsa Begum, 25, spent most of her recent pregnancy in a two-room apartment on the third floor of a five-storey building in a densely populated neighborhood of Dhaka, Bangladesh. Her bedroom remained dark even during the day, she says, as neighboring residential buildings blocked sunlight and restricted the flow of fresh air through the windows. […]

mix_items.title: Fossil of extinct giant bird discovered in Flores cave, Indonesia
mix_items.summary: Archaeologists excavating Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores have identified a new species of extinct giant bird that roamed the region some 150,000 years ago, according to a recent study. The giant bird was a kind of megapode — large, chicken-like birds that today live in the broader Australasian region. These birds […]

mix_items.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

mix_items.title: The Great Barrier Reef's most notorious coral killer may actually be helping it
mix_items.summary: Crown-of-thorns starfish are notorious for devouring coral reefs, but surprising new research reveals these spiny predators may actually help reefs thrive when their populations are kept in check. Scientists studying Australia's Great Barrier Reef discovered that nearly 75% of observed starfish feeding events left behind living coral tissue, rather than destroying entire colonies. By feeding on fast-growing, dominant corals, the starfish create opportunities for slower-growing species to survive, potentially increasing coral biodiversity.

mix_items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
mix_items.summary: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

mix_items.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches.

mix_items.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
mix_items.summary: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa.
